notes.original: Ouide au li. ij. de Ponto.
notes.gloss: The four lines translated in the text: Illud amicitiae quondam venerabile nomen / prostat et in quaestu pro meretrice sedet. / Diligitur nemo, nisi cui fortuna secunda est: / quae simul intonuit, proxima quaeque fugat. The print set no marker after the verse.

english.html: Nay, even of those in whom one may place some trust, they are found with such difficulty that the Phoenix at times is not so rare: indeed in this time the disgraces in friendship are so great that many profess intimate friendship with us, and show themselves outwardly more than ours, whose spirit and understanding are nonetheless disloyal, full of every treachery, and on every side our adversary: and under the honest cloak of friendship are our great enemies, worse certainly, and more dangerous, than those who openly declare themselves such <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>. For what plague could one imagine more violent, pernicious, or more effective to harm, than a familiar enemy <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>, who has irreparably injured us before we suspect him? whereas we can easily avoid him who openly shows himself our adversary <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>. That is why one must be very prudent in choosing a friend, and eat a hogshead of salt with a man — that is, converse long with him — before placing one's trust in him and committing to him anything of one's most secret matters <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>. Debate your cause (said the Sage) with your friend, and do not reveal your secrets to another: lest perchance he who hears you reproach you with it, and that blame return upon you <sup class="mk" data-key="k">k</sup>. A stricter maxim is further attributed to Bias, namely that one should so love a person as to think that one might also some day hate him <sup class="mk" data-key="l">l</sup>; which Publilius the Mime-writer afterwards took over among his gravest maxims, saying:

english.html: Ita amicum habeas, posse ut fieri inimicum putes.

Hold your friend in such rank that you reckon he may in the future be your enemy. Words which, as Scipio writes in the works of Cicero, are the most hostile to friendship that one could devise, and so barbarous that he could not persuade himself that Bias, one of the seven sages and so renowned, had spewed them out. For how is it possible that you should be the true friend of one whose enemy you fear to be in the future <sup class="mk" data-key="m">m</sup>? It is quite true that, as there is nothing permanent in this world <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup>, friendship at all times and in all persons cannot be lasting until the

notes.gloss: Scipio's rejection of the maxim "love as if you would one day hate," which he cannot believe was Bias's; the line Ita amicum habeas … is Publilius Syrus, Sententiae I 16.

notes.citation: Digest 8.2 (De servitutibus praediorum urbanorum) or Code 3.34 (De servitutibus et de aqua), l. Cum debere; fragment not identified

lines: Quæ ſimul intonuit, proxima quæque fugat.
Meſmes que de ceux, eſquels on peut colloquer quel
que fiance, ils ſ'en trouuent ſi difficillement, que le Phe-
nix quelquefois, n'eſt pas ſi rare: voire en ce temps, les
diſgraces en amitié ſont ſi grandes, que pluſieurs font
profeſsion auec nous d'intime amitié, & ſe monſtrent,
exterieurement pluſque noſtres, deſquels neantmoins l'e
prit & l'entendement eſt deſloyal: plein de de toute pro
dition, & de toutes parts noſtré aduerſaire: & ſous l'hon
neſte manteau d'amitié, ſont nos grans ennemis: plus
mauuais certes, & dangereux, que ceux qui pour tels
ouuertement ſe declarent {f}. Car quelle peſte pourroit
on ſonger plus violente, pernicieuſe, ni plus efficace à
nuire, qu'vn familier ennemy {g}, lequel nous à irrepara-
blemẽt offenſez, auant que ſe doubter de luy? ou toures
fois, nous pouuons facilemẽt euiter celuy, qui ouuerte-
ment ſe monſtre noſtre aduerſaire {h}. Voila pourquoy:
faut bien eſtre prudent, à choiſir vn ami. & manger vn
muy de ſel auec vn homme: c'eſt à dire, conuerſer lon-
guement auec luy, auant qu'y mettre ſa fiance, & luy
commettre rien des choſes plus ſecrettes {i}. Traite ta cau
ſe (diſoit le Sage) auec ton ami, & ne reuele point tes
ſecrets à vn autre: que parauenture celuy qui t'eſcoute, ne
te le reproche, & que ce blaſme ne retourne ſur toy {k}. On
attribue encore à Bias, vne ſentẽce plus eſtroite, à ſçauoir
qu'il conuenoit tellement aimer vne perſonne, qu'on pen
ſaſt auſſi quelque iour le hayr {l}. ce que Publius Mimus
entre ſes plus graues ſentences, apres vſurpa, diſant.
Ita amicum habeas, poſſe vt fieri inimicũ putes.
Ayes ton ami en tel reng. que tu cuides qu'il peut à
l'aduenir eſtre ton ennemy. Paroles ainſi que Scipion eſ
crit aux œuures de Ciceron, les plus ennemis de l'ami-
tié qu'on pourrit excogiter: & ſi barbares, qu'il ne ſe pou
roit perſuader, que Bias, vn des ſept ſages, & tant renom-
mé les euſt vomies. Car comme eſt il poſſible, que tu
ſois vray ami de celuy, duquel tu crains, à l'aduenir eſtre
ſon ennemy {m}? Il eſt bien vray que comme il n'y a rien
de permanent en ce mõde {n}. l'amitié en tout temps & en
toutes perſonnes, ne peut pas eſtre perdurable, iuſqu'au
